dimensions.name: Contract extraction & environment probing

evidence.note: Environment probing: checks python3/node/npm/pip availability, python version + installed packages, installs aiohttp/aiosqlite, confirms runtime constraints before designing. No explicit Chromium/browser probe despite CUA grading.

Explicitly extracted and verified the dense-per-channel-seq-across-writers invariant (web seq=1, IRC seq=2) and that seq stays dense (1-5) after broadcaster kill — a subtle load-bearing contract, actively confirmed.

Pulled specific spec edges from memory into checks: /me kept literally as '/me <text>', empty-message no-blank-post validation, and the workspace-general-submit testid — showing targeted contract recall beyond generic CRUD.
Systematically cross-referenced the served SPA against the full data-testid list from the spec, diagnosing false 'missing' matches as regex artifacts rather than real gaps.
Verified explicit status codes (400 invalid username, 409 duplicate) and node_id 0/1/2 port indexing against the health contract.

Extraction is done inline as build/verify analysis notes rather than as a distilled, revisited contract inventory; deepest traps (transfer-ownership vs PATCH-to-owner, guest/member/admin channel gates, non-member mention exclusion, resume.gap) are not surfaced or reasoned about explicitly.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent confirmed the runtime (language, framework, packages, listening ports) and caught most explicit status codes, envelope keys, and testids — clearly at the level-5 bar — and went beyond it by surfacing several genuinely subtle traps (dense-seq-across-writers verified live, /me literal body, node_id port indexing, empty-message validation) and systematically cross-referencing the full testid list against the spec. However, it never produced a distilled, referenced contract inventory nor a living, revisited map, left several of the sharpest traps (transfer-ownership vs PATCH, guest/member/admin gates, non-member mention exclusion, resume.gap boundaries) unaddressed in the trajectory, and skipped probing for the browser. That places it solidly between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & milestone structure

evidence.note: Opening plan lays out a dependency-aware architecture: shared SQLite seq store, 3 HTTP nodes, IRC gateway, and a dedicated broadcaster process with SQLite-polling fallback for fan-out. The critical shared substrate (dense per-channel seq + cross-node transport with degraded-mode fallback) is identified up front, and start.sh is authored as a first-class entry/supervision concern early (step 4) rather than bolted on.

Build order is dependency-correct: db schema → util → serializers → events/broadcaster → server.py (auth routes first, then users/workspaces/channels/messages) → IRC → supervisor → SPA HTML/JS. Foundations precede dependents and the API precedes the SPA. However, this is a big-bang code-writing phase; the 'Plan' lines are next-step notes, not enumerated milestones with written acceptance criteria.

Verification is batched at the end rather than per-subsystem, but it deliberately targets the highest-risk cross-cutting invariants in a sensible order: cross-node read, dense seq across web+IRC writers (36-37), broadcaster-kill with seq staying dense (38-39), node-kill/restart (40), and cross-node WS fan-out (44). This shows the risky invariants were recognized as their own checkpoints.

Final smoke tests re-confirm health/node_ids, token, index, and process supervision before submitting — a closing done-check across the assembled system, though again as an end-of-build batch rather than milestone-by-milestone gating.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced a sensible, dependency-correct breakdown (auth→workspaces/channels→messages→WS→IRC→SPA→resilience) and, notably, recognized the load-bearing shared substrate — dense per-channel seq plus a fan-out transport with a polling fallback — and treated start.sh/supervision as a first-class early concern, which pushes above the pure-5 anchor. It falls short of 8 because there is no explicit milestone hierarchy with written per-milestone exit criteria and dependencies made visible throughout; the work was a big-bang build with verification of subsystems (including the high-risk seq/resilience invariants) deferred to a single end-phase rather than gated milestone-by-milestone. That places the observed behavior between the 5 and 8 anchors, at a 6.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification across protocols

evidence.note: Ad-hoc curl e2e: register, workspace, channel, message, cross-node read (post on 8000 visible on 8001), plus 400/409 status-code checks — real HTTP-envelope verification.
Drove IRC via a Python socket script (no nc available): PASS/NICK/USER/JOIN/PRIVMSG, then verified web seq=1 vs IRC seq=2 — direct confirmation of dense per-channel seq under mixed HTTP+IRC writers.

Actively simulated BOTH grader failure scenarios: SIGKILL'd the broadcaster and confirmed seq stayed dense (1-5) across nodes within the window; SIGKILL'd an HTTP node and confirmed auto-restart plus continued service on the other two.
WebSocket cross-node fan-out test: subscribe on 8002, receive a message posted on 8000 — verifies delivery across nodes, though resume.gap/exactly-once were not exercised.
SPA verification was only static: curl the served JS and grep for testid presence, not an actual browser-driven pass against the pinned selectors — a real gap in transport coverage.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent built targeted checks across HTTP, WS, and IRC and — the distinguishing level-8 behavior — actively killed both an HTTP node and the broadcast component, confirming continued writes and dense seq within the stated windows, plus dense seq under mixed HTTP+IRC writers. It falls short of a full 8/10 because the SPA transport was only eyeballed via grep rather than browser-driven, resume.gap/exactly-once/tombstone semantics went untested, and the checks were throwaway snippets rather than a reusable harness. That places it firmly above the level-5 'resilience thin/omitted' anchor but below the 'reusable checks spanning all four transports' bar of 8.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across a huge feature surface

evidence.note: During the build, each step's Plan line functions as a running queue of the next subsystem to write (auth→workspace→channels→messages→reactions→files→search→invitations→groups→read-state→ws→IRC→supervisor→SPA), giving coarse but consistent orientation over what has been built vs. what remains, so no whole feature family is dropped from the build.

Explicitly enumerated the spec's testid list and grepped the served JS to find which selectors might be missing, then reconciled apparent 'missing' hits as a regex artifact — a deliberate cross-check of implementation against the spec's contract list (coverage verification).
Caught a concrete omission — a duplicated data-testid (workspace-general-submit) — and patched it, showing it was tracking contract-level detail rather than assuming completeness.

Verification phase walked subsystem-by-subsystem (seq density across web+IRC, broadcaster-kill fan-out, node-kill restart, cross-node WS resume, duplicate-channel 409), demonstrating subsystem-granularity progress tracking of the load-bearing invariants.

Final wrap-up recites the component inventory but the verification never revisits several built families (search, groups, invitations, read-state, mentions) — they are assumed working, so the done/partial/failing picture is incomplete at the feature-verification level; no explicit continuously-updated ledger exists.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained subsystem-level orientation throughout — its Plan lines form a running build queue and its test phase marches through most major invariants, catching a real omission (duplicate testid) and performing an explicit testid-vs-spec cross-check (steps 50-52), which is stronger than the level-5 anchor's 'generally knows what's left.' But it never kept an explicit, continuously-updated done/partial/failing ledger, and whole built families (search, groups, read-state, invitations) were assumed complete without verification, falling short of the level-8 anchor. There was little thrashing to detect, so no evidence of stuck-state naming. This lands at 6, between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified design assumptions

evidence.note: Upfront chose seq allocation in SQLite (single durable authority) with broadcaster as a mere fast fan-out layer and SQLite polling as fallback — the exact robust design anchor 10 describes, but decided proactively rather than after a falsified assumption.

Proactively stress-tested the riskiest invariant early: killed the broadcaster, posted messages from multiple nodes, and confirmed dense seq (1,2,3,4,5) held across nodes. This matches the 'proactively stress-tests risky design assumptions early' half of anchor 10 — but the test passed, so no correction was needed.
Continued proactive failure-injection tests (kill an HTTP node → verify auto-restart; cross-node WS fan-out) — all passed on first try, so no divergence surfaced and no re-architecture occurred.
The only actual correction observed was a minor, local patch (duplicate data-testid fix), unrelated to seq/resilience design — a targeted symptom fix, not a design revision.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent proactively stress-tested exactly the fragile invariants (seq density under broadcaster-kill, node restart, cross-node WS fan-out), which is the 'proactively stress-tests risky assumptions early' behavior described in anchor 10, and its upfront design (durable seq authority in SQLite) already embodied the robust choice that anchor praises. However, because every stress test passed on the first attempt, reality never diverged and no re-architecture-on-falsification was ever observed; the sole correction (a testid patch, steps 46-47) was minor and local. Observed behavior thus sits above the '5' targeted-correction anchor due to genuine proactive stress-testing, but below '8' because no falsified assumption ever triggered a design revision to witness.

dimensions.name: Grader-value scope triage under budget

evidence.note: In the design phase the agent front-loaded the highest-risk architecture: cross-node fan-out via a broadcaster with an SQLite-polling fallback explicitly to survive the broadcaster-kill and keep seq dense. This targets the resilience/seq invariants that gate many grader checks rather than starting with cosmetic features.

Verification was sequenced to hit the load-bearing invariants first — cross-node read, IRC/web shared dense seq, broadcaster-kill with seq staying dense (1..5), node SIGKILL + auto-restart, and cross-node WS fan-out — showing awareness of which systems carry the most grader weight.
Ran a dedicated pass comparing the served SPA's data-testid set against the pinned spec list, recognizing the testids as a high-coverage gating surface for the Playwright/CUA grader.

Reasoned in grader-coverage terms ('the grader probably tests...', 'the verifier will SIGKILL one node') about specific checks (empty-message validation, /me literal body, resilience windows), but built the full feature surface uniformly with no explicit defer/stub/minimal-viable calls on low-value features.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent clearly targets the big-ticket, clearly-graded systems first — auth/API, the dense seq invariant, resilience/fan-out, and the pinned testids — and its design and verification both front-load these high-coverage, high-risk areas (above pure level 5). However, it treats the whole feature set as required and builds it all in dependency order without articulating conscious value/risk weighting, deferral, stubbing, or budget reallocation as verification reveals marginal value, which the level-8 anchor demands. This places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at a 6.

rubric.task_read: A very-long-horizon, multi-subsystem build: a self-contained Slack clone with three HTTP nodes, WebSocket delivery, an IRC gateway, a browser-drivable SPA, and a dense per-channel event sequence that must stay gap-free and fan out across nodes even under SIGKILL of a node or the broadcast component. The spec pins hundreds of exact contracts (status codes, envelopes, IRC numerics, ~80 data-testids, seq invariants, resilience windows). Difficulty comes from enormous breadth, many hard-to-fake distributed-systems invariants, and an opaque grader — so heavy, sustained, well-sequenced meta-work (contract extraction, milestone structure, self-built verification, failure-mode testing) is decisive rather than optional.

dimensions.name: Contract extraction & environment probing
dimensions.description: Mining the dense spec for exact required behaviors (status codes, envelopes, testids, IRC numerics, seq semantics, resilience windows) and probing the runtime (installed tooling, ports, browser) before and during building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader asserts precise shapes across HTTP/WS/IRC/UI; a single mis-read contract (e.g. `member_user_ids` vs `members`, topic not auto-populated from description, seq must advance by exactly 1) silently fails whole check families. Blind coding here guarantees rework.

anchors.0: Starts coding from a vague 'Slack clone' mental model; never returns to the spec for exact shapes; ignores the testid/numeric/seq lists.
anchors.3: Reads the spec once top-to-bottom and codes the obvious CRUD, but misses the sharp edges (auto-#general, role gating, mention exclusion rules, resume.gap, node_id indexing) and never checks what's installed.
anchors.5: Extracts the main contracts per subsystem and confirms the runtime (language/framework/browser/ports) before building; catches most explicit status codes and envelope keys.
anchors.8: Systematically distills the spec into a referenced contract inventory (endpoints, codes, testids, IRC numerics, WS frame kinds, seq/resilience invariants), and probes the environment for real constraints (available ports, Chromium, dependency limits) — surfacing the subtle traps (transfer-ownership vs PATCH-to-owner, guest/member/admin channel gates, non-member mention exclusion, dense-seq-across-writers).
anchors.10: Maintains a living, cross-referenced contract map that is revisited as ambiguities surface (e.g. how DM idempotency, tombstoned-reaction counting, or resume.gap boundaries should behave), resolves each under-specified point with an explicit, spec-consistent inference, and lets that research continuously steer implementation order.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & milestone structure
dimensions.description: Breaking the system into ordered, independently-verifiable subsystems (auth → workspaces/channels → messages/threads/reactions → WS → IRC → SPA → clustering/resilience) each with an explicit done-check, and sequencing them so foundations exist before dependents.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The task is far too large for one undifferentiated push; without a dependency-aware milestone plan the agent risks building the SPA before the API works or resilience before the seq layer exists, and cannot tell what fraction is truly complete.

anchors.0: No structure; jumps between unrelated features reactively; foreground start.sh and clustering treated as afterthoughts.
anchors.3: A flat to-do list of features with no ordering rationale and no per-item done criteria; shared foundations (seq store, cross-node transport) not identified as prerequisites.
anchors.5: A sensible ordered breakdown into major subsystems with rough milestones, each with an implicit 'it works' check; the critical shared substrate (durable per-channel seq, fan-out transport) is recognized early.
anchors.8: Explicit milestone hierarchy with per-milestone acceptance checks, dependencies made visible (auth/token before everything; seq+persistence before WS/IRC/resilience; API before SPA), and start.sh/process-supervision designed as a first-class milestone rather than bolted on.
anchors.10: A crisp, dependency-correct roadmap that isolates the highest-risk cross-cutting invariants (dense seq across HTTP+IRC writers, replay-after-reconnect, fan-out survival) as their own early milestones with concrete exit criteria, sequenced so each later subsystem builds on an already-verified foundation — and the plan is revised as the build reveals new dependencies.

dimensions.name: Self-built verification across protocols
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing checks the grader won't hand you: curl/HTTP assertions on codes and envelopes, WebSocket subscribe/resume/seq tests, IRC socket sessions, SPA driving, and — critically — actively simulating the SIGKILL and broadcast-kill resilience scenarios.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The grader is opaque and covers HTTP+WS+IRC+browser+failure injection. Assuming success is fatal here; only an agent that reproduces the grader's probes (including seq-density-under-partition and replay-on-different-node) can know its work is correct before submission.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'the server starts'; never exercises endpoints, WS frames, IRC, the UI, or any failure scenario.
anchors.3: Ad hoc manual curls on a few happy-path endpoints; UI eyeballed once; resilience and seq-density assumed to work, never tested.
anchors.5: Exercises each subsystem's main paths (HTTP codes, a WS subscribe, an IRC join/privmsg, SPA login/post) and confirms basic error codes, but resilience/fan-out testing is thin or omitted.
anchors.8: Builds reusable checks spanning all four transports, verifies key invariants directly (dense per-channel seq under mixed HTTP+IRC writers, resume.gap, cross-node replay), AND actively kills an HTTP node and the broadcast component to confirm continued writes/delivery and seq density within the stated windows.
anchors.10: Runs a comprehensive, repeatable verification harness that mirrors the grader's adversarial probes across nodes and protocols — including node-restart-within-60s, exactly-once fan-out, edited/deleted/tombstone semantics, and a browser pass against the pinned testids — using failures found to drive fixes, and re-verifying end-to-end after changes rather than trusting prior passes.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across a huge feature surface
dimensions.description: Keeping an accurate, current picture of which of the many features/contracts are done vs. remaining vs. broken across a long build, and detecting stuck or circular states (e.g. re-debugging seq gaps repeatedly).
dimensions.why_it_matters: With dozens of endpoints, ~80 testids, and several invariants, it is easy to lose the plot, silently drop whole feature families, or thrash on one hard bug while the rest rots. Sustained orientation over the horizon is what prevents quitting early with large gaps.

anchors.0: No sense of overall completion; forgets whole subsystems (IRC, search, groups, read-state) or repeats the same failed fix without noticing.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of progress; discovers late that major areas were never built; no signal for being stuck.
anchors.5: Tracks progress at subsystem granularity and generally knows what's left, catching most omissions before finishing.
anchors.8: Maintains an explicit, continuously-updated status of features/contracts (done / partial / failing), notices when a fix isn't converging and names the stuck state, and uses that ledger to decide what to touch next.
anchors.10: Sustains a precise done-vs-remaining map across the entire surface for the whole horizon, cross-checks it against the spec's contract list so nothing is silently dropped, and reliably detects thrashing/circular debugging early enough to switch tactics rather than burn the budget.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified design assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising the architecture or approach when reality diverges — e.g. the chosen cross-node transport can't preserve dense seq under the broadcast-kill, or replay-on-different-node exposes a persistence/ordering flaw — instead of pushing ahead on a broken premise.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Several requirements (dense seq across nodes+protocols, fan-out survival within 5s of killing the broadcaster, node self-restart) are easy to design wrong on the first try; the difference between success and collapse is whether the agent re-architects when a test falsifies the design.

anchors.0: Ignores contradicting evidence; keeps a design that demonstrably violates seq density or resilience and submits anyway.
anchors.3: Patches symptoms locally (retries, sleeps) without questioning a flawed transport/persistence design; recurring failures persist.
anchors.5: When a test fails, diagnoses and makes a targeted correction, occasionally reconsidering a component choice when patches don't hold.
anchors.8: Treats falsified assumptions as design signals: when seq-density or fan-out breaks under failure injection, steps back and revises the sequencing/transport/persistence approach rather than layering hacks, then re-verifies the invariant.
anchors.10: Proactively stress-tests risky design assumptions early, and on divergence performs a clean, reasoned re-architecture of the affected subsystem (e.g. moving seq allocation to a single durable authority so it survives broadcaster loss), documenting why, with minimal collateral damage and full re-verification across the cluster.

dimensions.name: Grader-value scope triage under budget
dimensions.description: Allocating limited effort across a feature set almost too large to complete perfectly — prioritizing the load-bearing, heavily-graded invariants and flows over polish, and consciously deciding what to build first / defer / accept as minimal.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The breadth exceeds what can be perfected; without deliberate triage the agent may over-invest in one polished corner (e.g. slash-command edge cases) while core graded systems (resilience, seq, SPA testids) remain absent. Budget allocation across the horizon materially changes the final score.

anchors.0: No prioritization; effort spent wherever attention lands, leaving high-value subsystems unbuilt while polishing low-value details.
anchors.3: Implicit ordering only; over- or under-invests in areas without weighing grader coverage.
anchors.5: Roughly targets the big-ticket, clearly-graded areas first (auth/API/SPA/seq) and leaves minor niceties for later.
anchors.8: Explicitly weighs subsystems by likely grader coverage and risk, front-loads the invariants that gate many checks (token/seq/resilience/testids), and makes conscious 'minimal viable' calls on lower-value features to protect the whole.
anchors.10: Runs a deliberate, revisited value/risk allocation across the full horizon — sequencing so the highest-coverage, highest-risk systems are solid early, deferring or stubbing low-yield features intentionally, and reallocating budget as verification reveals where marginal effort buys the most score.
